title: How the Silk Road Actually Worked (and What Could Go Terribly Wrong On It)
description: You don’t have to spend a long time read­ing up on the Silk Road before you see the term itself (“Silk Road”) called a mis­nomer. In fact, wh
body:
You don’t have to spend a long time read­ing up on the Silk Road before you see the term itself (“Silk Road”) called a mis­nomer. In fact, what we refer to by that name com­pris­es a whole net­work of trade routes con­nect­ing Asia, Africa, and Europe, whose traf­fic con­stant­ly shift­ed over a mil­len­ni­um and a half accord­ing to cli­mat­ic, geopo­lit­i­cal, and civ­i­liza­tion­al con­di­tions. Nor was silk the only, or even the pri­ma­ry type of good car­ried along those routes. From East to West went tea, dyes, per­fumes, porce­lain, and paper; from West to East, glass­ware, hors­es, camels, hon­ey, wine, and gold, to name just a few items in peren­ni­al demand. It was along the Silk Road, or Silk-and-Many-Oth­er-Things-Roads, that gun­pow­der spread out of Chi­na — and the Black Death spread out of Europe.
Accord­ing to the Knowl­ed­gia video above, the rough­ly 4,000-mile-long Silk Road was offi­cial­ly opened in 130 BC. But it was­n’t with­out its pre­de­ces­sors: in 500 BC, for exam­ple, the “Roy­al Road” estab­lished by Dar­ius I’s Achaemenid Empire “stretched from Susa, which lies in mod­ern-day Iran, all the way, near­ly 2,000 miles to the west, to Sardis, which is today a part of Turkey,” with spurs reach­ing India and North­ern Africa.
What­ev­er its eco­nom­ic impact, the Roy­al Road had noth­ing like the cul­tur­al effects of the Silk Road, any his­to­ry of which empha­sizes the “new think­ing and new ways of life being passed along the net­work of trade routes,” to say noth­ing of “the spread of reli­gions or ide­olo­gies that would occur thanks to the mer­chants and trav­el­ers them­selves.”


	

This despite the fact that few of those mer­chants or trav­el­ers crossed the Silk Road­’s entire length. But we can all name at least one man who made the full jour­ney: the thir­teenth-cen­tu­ry Venet­ian explor­er Mar­co Polo, who as a teenag­er first made the trek to Kublai Khan’s plea­sure dome with his father. (At that point, the Mon­gol Empire had already uni­fied its routes, but not before lay­ing waste to a fair few set­tle­ments along the way.) It is to Polo’s writ­ings that we owe our endur­ing­ly roman­tic image of the Silk Road, but he under­stood the dan­gers of that law­less gaunt­let across empires as well as any­one. The Urban Atlas video above lists a few of them, includ­ing desert heat, dis­eases, hal­lu­ci­na­tions, ban­dit­ry, and slav­ery. Today, we encounter no such per­ils on the way from Rome to Xi’an, a jour­ney we can make on a flight with a stopover in Bei­jing. Per­haps Mar­co Polo would say we’ve all gone soft, but then, he’d prob­a­bly be more inter­est­ed in learn­ing about our roads in the sky.
Relat­ed con­tent:
The Inge­nious Engi­neer­ing of Silk: How the 2,000-Year-Old Pat­tern Loom Pow­ered the Silk Road and the Wealth of Ancient Chi­na
Behold an Incred­i­bly Detailed, Hand­made Map Of Medieval Trade Routes
Invis­i­ble Cities Illus­trat­ed: Artist Illus­trates Each and Every City in Ita­lo Calvino’s Clas­sic Nov­el
The Most Dis­tant Places Vis­it­ed by the Romans: Africa, Scan­di­navia, Chi­na, India, Ara­bia & Oth­er Far-Flung Lands

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: How Martin Luther King, Jr. Used Nietzsche, Hegel & Kant to Overturn Segregation in America
description:
Image by Dick DeMar­si­co, via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
The influ­ence of Georg Wil­helm Friedrich Hegel on the rev­o­lu­tion­ary phi­los­o­phy of Ka
body:
Image by Dick DeMar­si­co, via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
The influ­ence of Georg Wil­helm Friedrich Hegel on the rev­o­lu­tion­ary phi­los­o­phy of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels is well known. Marx wrote a cri­tique of Hegel’s Phi­los­o­phy of Right and claimed to have turned the Ger­man ide­al­ist philoso­pher on his head, and the devel­op­ment of Marx­ist the­o­ry among a school of neo-Hegelians, wrote Rebec­ca Coop­er in 1925, occurred in a peri­od “pecu­liar­ly aus­pi­cious for the birth of a rev­o­lu­tion­ary social phi­los­o­phy.”
A cen­tu­ry lat­er, on anoth­er con­ti­nent, Hegel’s thought influ­enced the course of a very dif­fer­ent strug­gle. And while the his­tor­i­cal con­di­tions of mid-nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry Europe and mid-twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­ca present entire­ly dif­fer­ent sets of spe­cif­ic con­cerns, the same gen­er­al obser­va­tion applies: the time and place of such rad­i­cal thinkers as Mal­colm X, Angela Davis, Huey New­ton and a host of oth­er activists pre­sent­ed “pecu­liar­ly aus­pi­cious” cir­cum­stances for rev­o­lu­tion­ary social phi­los­o­phy.
But while these fig­ures appear today as the van­guard of rad­i­cal black thought, Mar­tin Luther King, Jr., the most wide­ly cel­e­brat­ed of Civ­il Rights lead­ers, “is often con­flat­ed with neolib­er­al mul­ti­cul­tur­al­ism,” writes Crit­i­cal The­o­ry, his pro­gram asso­ci­at­ed with “the fail­ure of the civ­il rights move­ment to dis­man­tle the ongo­ing sys­temic white suprema­cy of the sta­tus quo.” And yet, King’s move­ment not only suc­ceed­ed in end­ing legal seg­re­ga­tion and has­ten­ing the pass­ing of the Civ­il Rights Act; it also pro­vid­ed direc­tion for near­ly every non­vi­o­lent social move­ment from his day to ours. King’s lega­cy is not only that of an inspir­ing orga­niz­er and ora­tor, but also of a rad­i­cal thinker who engaged crit­i­cal­ly with phi­los­o­phy and social the­o­ry and brought it to bear on his activism.
We are gen­er­al­ly well aware of King’s debt to Gand­hi and the Satya­gra­ha move­ment that won Indi­an inde­pen­dence in 1947, yet we know lit­tle of his debt to the same thinker who inspired Marx and his contemporaries—G.W.F. Hegel. As philoso­pher Nolen Gertz has demon­strat­ed on his blog, King was high­ly influ­enced by Hegelian­ism, as much as, or per­haps even more so, than he was by Gand­hi’s move­ment. Marx may have turned Hegel’s sys­tem on its head, but King, writes Gertz, “fought White Amer­i­ca… by turn­ing the ideas of dead white men against the oppres­sive prac­tices of liv­ing white men.”

King read and wrote on Hegel as a grad­u­ate stu­dent at Boston Uni­ver­si­ty and Har­vard in the mid-’50s, where he stud­ied the­ol­o­gy and the his­to­ry of phi­los­o­phy and reli­gion. He took a year­long sem­i­nar on Hegel with his advi­sor at BU, Edgar Bright­man (see King’s dia­gram notes of Hegel’s sys­tem above), and found a great deal to admire in the “dead white” philosopher’s log­i­cal sys­tem, as well as a good deal to cri­tique. The two-semes­ter class, King wrote in his auto­bi­og­ra­phy, was “both reward­ing and stim­u­lat­ing”:
Although the course was main­ly a study of Hegel’s mon­u­men­tal work, Phe­nom­e­nol­o­gy of Mind, I spent my spare time read­ing his Phi­los­o­phy of His­to­ry and Phi­los­o­phy of Right. There were points in Hegel’s phi­los­o­phy that I strong­ly dis­agreed with. For instance, his absolute ide­al­ism was ratio­nal­ly unsound to me because it tend­ed to swal­low up the many in the one. But there were oth­er aspects of his think­ing that I found stim­u­lat­ing. His con­tention that “truth is the whole” led me to a philo­soph­i­cal method of ratio­nal coher­ence. His analy­sis of the dialec­ti­cal process, in spite of its short­com­ings, helped me to see that growth comes through strug­gle.
While King may have dis­agreed with Hegel’s ide­al­ism, he found sup­port for his own phi­los­o­phy of non­vi­o­lence in Hegel’s dialec­ti­cal method, a mode of analy­sis that seems par­tic­u­lar­ly well suit­ed to social­ly rev­o­lu­tion­ary thought. In Stride Toward Free­dom, King wrote,
The third way open to oppressed peo­ple in their quest for free­dom is the way of non­vi­o­lent resis­tance. Like the syn­the­sis in Hegelian phi­los­o­phy, the prin­ci­ple of non­vi­o­lent resis­tance seeks to rec­on­cile the truths of two opposites—acquiescence and violence—while avoid­ing the extremes and immoral­i­ties of both.
King’s crit­i­cal appraisal of Hegel extend­ed to oth­er rad­i­cal philo­soph­i­cal thinkers as well, includ­ing Kant, Spin­oza, Kierkegaard, Marx, and Niet­zsche. Gertz offers many sam­ples of the bud­ding Civ­il Rights leader’s notes on var­i­ous thinkers and philoso­phies, includ­ing the first para­graph of an essay enti­tled “Pil­grim­age to Non­vi­o­lence” (below), in which King con­fess­es that his encounter with Exis­ten­tial­ism often “shocked” him, espe­cial­ly since he had “been raised in a rather strict fun­da­men­tal­ist tra­di­tion.” And yet, he writes—in an allu­sion to Kant’s reac­tion to David Hume—he acquired “a new appre­ci­a­tion for objec­tive appraisal and crit­i­cal analy­sis” that “knocked me out of my dog­mat­ic slum­ber.”

In the essay, King writes, “I became con­vinced that exis­ten­tial­ism, in spite of the fact that it had become all too fash­ion­able, had grasped cer­tain basic truths about man.” He seems par­tic­u­lar­ly drawn to Kierkegaard (see his notes on the philoso­pher below). Yet it is Hegel who seems most respon­si­ble for awak­en­ing his philo­soph­i­cal curios­i­ty. As King schol­ar John Ans­bro dis­cov­ered, King “stat­ed in a Jan­u­ary 19, 1956 inter­view with The Mont­gomery Adver­tis­er that Hegel was his favorite philoso­pher.” Lat­er that year, King gave an address to the First Annu­al Insti­tute on Non­vi­o­lence and Social Change in which he used Hegelian terms to char­ac­ter­ize the Civ­il Rights strug­gle: “Long ago, the Greek philoso­pher Her­a­cli­tus argued that jus­tice emerges from the strife of oppo­sites, and Hegel, in mod­ern phi­los­o­phy, preached a doc­trine of growth through strug­gle.”

Inde­pen­dent schol­ar Ralph Dumain has fur­ther cat­a­logued King’s many approv­ing ref­er­ences to Hegel, includ­ing a paper he wrote enti­tled “An Expo­si­tion of the First Tri­ad of Cat­e­gories of the Hegelian Logic—Being, Non-Being, Becom­ing,” the “last of six essays that King wrote” for his two-semes­ter course on the philoso­pher. King also approached Hegel by way of an ear­li­er Civ­il Rights leader—W.E.B. Du Bois, who read the Ger­man philoso­pher while study­ing with promi­nent social sci­en­tists in Berlin, and who applied Hegelian log­ic to his own analy­sis of racial con­scious­ness and strug­gle in Amer­i­ca.
Inter­est­ing­ly, what nei­ther King nor Du Bois remarked on is the fact that Hegel was like­ly him­self inspired by black rev­o­lu­tion­ar­ies. The Hait­ian Rev­o­lu­tion, argues schol­ar Susan Buck-Morss, gave Hegel the impe­tus for his analy­sis of pow­er and his “metaphor of the ‘strug­gle to death’ between the mas­ter and slave, which for Hegel pro­vid­ed the key to the unfold­ing of free­dom in world his­to­ry.” While Hegel’s thought is a philo­soph­i­cal thread that winds through the work of rad­i­cal thinkers through­out the nine­teenth and twen­ti­eth cen­turies, his own phi­los­o­phy may not have tak­en the direc­tion it did with­out the rev­o­lu­tion­ary strug­gles against oppres­sion waged by for­mer slaves in the New World cen­turies before King led his non­vi­o­lent war on the oppres­sive sys­tem of seg­re­ga­tion in the Unit­ed States.
H/T Nolen Gertz
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: The Battle of New York
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                Artists reflect on 25 years since 9/11, Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch calls it quits, and
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Artists reflect on 25 years since 9/11, Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch calls it quits, and our list of art books to read this fall.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            September 7, noon: It’s Labor Day but some labor has to be done. I see a young man at a cafe wearing a hat embroidered with the words “Contemporary Art Market.” If only he knew, I mutter, and bury my head back into my laptop. September 8, morning: I meet Chilean artist Alfredo Jaar in Chelsea. We talk about the rise of authoritarianism, the decline of democracy, and other depressing things. In the evening, this gloominess turns cathartic as he delivers a moving lecture at the CUNY Graduate Center in Manhattan. They serve a buffet but I don’t touch any of it. On my way out, I stop in front of an exhibit in the hallway to educate myself about the Battle of New York in 1776. Outside, the Empire State Building is lit in red, blue, and gold. Turns out it’s to mark the 60th anniversary of Star Trek. Zohran T-shirts are still going strong in tourist souvenir shops. On Park Avenue, I pass by the ugliest public art I’ve ever seen. But I’ve never loved a city as much as I love New York.           September 9, evening: We throw a pizza-and-wine party for Hyperallergic contributors at our Brooklyn office. I meet the loveliest people. Some days, everyone just seems beautiful to me. September 10, afternoon: We publish our first Pocket Review. These are fast, opinionated reviews of up to 300 words to read on the go. In the evening, I hop between several openings in Chelsea, including Johanna Unzueta’s sublime drawings at Casey Kaplan and a posthumous show of Yvonne Jacquette’s stunning aerial paintings at Karma. At the latter, I meet painter Katherine Bradford, who is looking for her lost purse. September 11, morning: A single-shot espresso at 7am. A double at 8:30am, and a large drip to sip on for the rest of the day. Kaveh Akbar’s Martyr plays in my headphones. Between two trees, One World Trade Center appears on the horizon. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief 


	
		
		Artists Reflect on 9/11 and the Wounds of the “War on Terror”
		
	
	
		Every year on September 11, New Yorkers pay tribute to the victims of the 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center — and to the wounds of the weeks and years after. That period was defined by grief, rebuilding efforts, and, almost immediately, a vicious campaign of Islamophobia and surveillance whose effects reshaped the world as they knew it. Iraqi-born artist Wafaa Bilal recalls, “I sensed at once that the comfort and security Americans had long taken for granted were gone.”

Bilal is one of several artists from Muslim, South Asian, and Southwest Asian and North African (SWANA) communities whose lives were indelibly altered by the United States’s weaponization of the 9/11 attacks to pass the PATRIOT Act and justify the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan. Twenty-five years into “never forget,” Hyperallergic asked artists, curators, and culture workers to share personal and artistic reflections on how that day shaped their lives. These are their stories. | Lakshmi Rivera Amin

title: Trump Demands ‘Strange Modernist’ Sculpture Be Replaced by George Washington Statue
description: President Donald Trump has released his latest list of demands for the Smithsonian Institution, beginning with the installation of a monumental stat
body:
President Donald Trump has released his latest list of demands for the Smithsonian Institution, beginning with the installation of a monumental statue of George Washington outside the National Museum of American History.

	In a flurry of Truth Social posts late Friday, Trump also called for an exhibition honoring the nation’s first president to open imminently and run through February 22, 2032, the 300th anniversary of Washington’s birth. The statue, Trump said, should be erected on September 17, Constitution Day in the United States. Standing at 11 feet, the work was featured at the recent Freedom 250 IndyCar race in the museum’s Flag Hall.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Writing en route to his golf course in Ireland, Trump also called for a 30-foot statue of Washington to replace Infinity, a kinetic sculpture by New York artist José de Rivera, dedicated by the federal government in 1967 and currently located at the south entrance of the National Museum of American History. 

	“Replace a sculpture that says nothing about America with the man who, more than anyone else, says everything about America,” Trump said, describing Washington as “easily America’s Greatest Hero. Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn’t exist.”

	Infinity was the first work of modern art commissioned by the US government under the Art and Architecture Program for the National Mall. The sculpture sits atop a black granite base and forms a ribbon of polished stainless steel that has continuously rotated since its dedication, completing one revolution every six minutes. De Rivera, whose sculptures mark public spaces across the United States, died in 1985.

	“That strange modernist sculpture tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes,” Trump said.

	In a separate post, the president accused the Smithsonian of failing to “give George Washington and our other Founding Fathers the celebration they deserve,” on the 250th anniversary of the nation’s independence. “Washington’s Heroic Crossing of the Delaware on December 25, 1776 — One of the greatest moments and turning points of the Revolution — is not even mentioned in the Museum,” he said.
	

	The Smithsonian National Museum of American History has several objects in its collection depicting Washington’s crossing of the Delaware, including a colored print by Thomas Kelly; a colored print based on Emanuel Gottlieb Leutze’s famous 1850 painting; an 1853 engraving titled Washington Crossing the Delaware, also based on Leutze’s painting; and a 2021 US quarter depicting Washington rallying his troops to cross the river. 

	It is unclear whether Trump has the authority to remove Infinity, since the Smithsonian operates independently of the executive branch. However, federal funds make up a significant portion of its annual budget, and it is overseen by a Board of Regents that includes Vice President JD Vance, who has spearheaded the Trump administration’s intervention in the museum network’s operations.

	Trump has repeatedly bypassed the congressional approval traditionally required to fundamentally change the Capitol’s cultural landscape. A divided Supreme Court recently allowed his ballroom project, which would replace the East Wing, to proceed, with the dissenting justices describing its construction as “likely unlawful.” Meanwhile, a towering sculpture by Joel Shapiro that had been on view at the Kennedy Center since 2019, when the artist gave it to the center as a gift, was dismantled. 
	

	The Kennedy Center did not explain why it removed the work. Shapiro’s daughter told the Times that the artist would have been “alarmed” by the removal. The Shapiro work, a blue, stick-like figure, was ultimately purchased by the center’s former chairman, David Rubenstein.

	Trump’s demand came days after Smithsonian Institution Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III announced his retirement. For more than a year, Bunch and the Trump administration have clashed over accusations that the Smithsonian was presenting an unflattering view of American history—claims Bunch rejected, saying the institution’s exhibitions were grounded in rigorous scholarship.

	“Under recently ended leadership, the Smithsonian created a ‘Center for Restorative History,’ and commissioned a ‘Decolonization Plan,’ to focus attention overwhelmingly on those who have been oppressed, but there is almost no attention paid to those who triumphed over great oppression, and against great odds,” Trump posted on Friday.

	“One current exhibit describes the period of 1492 to 1776, including Christopher Columbus’s discovery of the New World, and the European settlement of America, as the ‘Great Unsettling’ of the Continent,” he said, adding, “That tells you all you need to know about how twisted the thinking is today at the Smithsonian.”

title: How Janine Antoni Simultaneously Disturbs and Delights
description: Janine Antoni’s hands descend over the eyes of a creamy-colored bust to the sound of water pouring from a faucet. Bubbles froth at the sculpture’s c
body:
Janine Antoni’s hands descend over the eyes of a creamy-colored bust to the sound of water pouring from a faucet. Bubbles froth at the sculpture’s chin and twinkle from grooves between sculpted strands of hair. She caresses the immobile features, then turns the statue to face her. In this 2003 video, little of the artist herself can be seen: A sliver of bare leg presses against the white enamel of a bathtub; her quick hands studiously encircle the simulated cartilage of the bust’s outer ear as she uses the tips of her thumbs to excavate soap from the concha. Then, it cuts to Antoni seated in her studio, her features the same as those of the bust. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	“For me, [this work is] about that conflict, that kind of love/hate relationship we have with our physical appearance,” she says. “And, really, the problem I have of looking in the mirror and thinking, ‘Is that who I am?’” Another cut reveals a chocolate version of the same statue. 

	The footage, which originally appeared in an Art21 feature, captures Antoni remaking a bust from Lick and Lather (1993), an installation commissioned for that year’s Venice Biennale that encompasses 14 busts mimicking neoclassical marbles, seven made from chocolate and seven from soap. Cast from a mold of the artist’s head and chest, the sculptures’ features wear away as the artist gently washes and devours her own effigy, an erasure accomplished through apparent acts of tenderness. The piece—now her best known—has been remade on a few occasions due to the intense responses it invites; during the Biennale, a young woman licked and bit some works’ noses off in an inadvertent collaboration. While nonconsensual, the girl’s gesture was not far from Antoni’s own response to the art that then dominated museums. 

	Antoni has chafed against the art historical canon since she first exploded onto New York’s art scene in the 1990s. Production, destruction, and gender are among her central themes—in her hands, they entangle and blur. Antoni is often misconstrued as a performance artist, perhaps because her objects bear palpable traces of the intimate and durational processes through which she molds and shapes them, operating as sensual surrogates for her body in space. 
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Materials for Antoni’s Lick and Lather series, including molds of her own bust and a large stock pot filled with melted chocolate.
									Photo Christopher Garcia Valle
	



	Last spring, when I visited her home and studio in Brooklyn’s Park Slope neighborhood, I observed that many of her works take verbs as their titles: Lick and Lather, Gnaw (1992), Moor (2001), Tear (2008). In reply, she mused that museum wall labels list only materials, not how a work is created. “We have lost our connection to the way the objects we are in contact with every day are made,” she said. “This alienates us from our world.”

	As an antidote to this material estrangement, Antoni uses her own body in the place of traditional tools. She has turned eyelashes and hair into paintbrushes, teeth and tongue into chisel and rasp, and bodies and bones into molds. While in her studio, Antoni and I sat surrounded by photographic works from her 2019 exhibition “I am fertile ground” at Brooklyn’s Green-Wood Cemetery. They show parts of the body—the sole of a foot, hands clasped in prayer, a hand resting against the lobe of an ear—and are housed in gilded frames, stamped by and molded from plastic casts of human bones of the kind found in anatomy classrooms and doctors’ offices. In our conversation, she described her fascination with the erotics of the traces a body leaves, comparing the forensic forms that her work takes to the warmth of a recently vacated seat. She framed her art as an interface between artist and audience, a mode of making space for another’s body to enter, adding, “The work is just an excuse to get close.”
	


			
			
			
	
			
					View of Janine Antoni’s installation I am fertile ground, 2019, in the Catacombs at Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn.
									Photo Christopher Burke/Courtesy Luhring Augustine, New York, and Anthony Meier, Mill Valley, Calif./©Janine Antoni
	



	BORN IN FREEPORT, Bahamas, in 1964 to Trinidadian parents, Antoni attributes her love of the body to her childhood in the Caribbean. While her mother kept house, her father worked as a physician at a clinic that he cofounded with his brothers. When, on occasion, neighbors would visit their home for emergency treatment, Antoni would play nurse, handing her father his tools while he attended to his patient. “He taught me the miraculousness of the body,” she reflected during our studio visit. 

	That sense of wonder was complicated in 1977, when, at the age of 13, Antoni left to attend a Catholic girl’s high school in West Palm Beach, Florida. Keenly conscious of the different ways in which a gesture might be read in the US versus the Bahamas, she began to understand the body as socially conditioned, responsive not only to cultural context but to gender, race, and class. 

	Thinking back to the concerns that motivated her as a young artist in the early 1990s, Antoni reflected, “In the early work, I was trying to understand how and why the world responds to me, given that I have this particular, gendered body.” Rooting works in persistent biological rhythms such as sleeping, eating, and bathing, she began to question differences in the body as it consumes and is consumed. Works like Loving Care (1993) and Butterfly Kisses (1996–99) saw the artist transform cosmetics and other beauty products into media for gestural mark-making, drawing attention to the commodified production of gender. 
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Loving Care, 1993, at Anthony d’Offay Gallery, London.
									Courtesy LuhringPhoto Prudence Cumming Associates. Augustine, New York/©Janine Antoni.
	



	Some of the same works also take on feminized gestures in the form of maintenance work and reproductive labor. In Loving Care, first staged live in 1993 at Anthony d’Offay Gallery in London, Antoni soaked her hair in a bucket of “natural black” hair dye from Clairol’s Loving Care trademark, the same brand used by her mother. On hands and knees, she “washed” the gallery floor with her dye-saturated hair, satirizing the gestural braggadocio of Abstract Expressionist action painting and the “human paintbrushes” of Yves Klein’s body prints. As black marks coated the gallery floor, onlookers were gradually expelled from the gallery. 

	THESE WORKS GREW in part out of vital lessons Antoni took from feminist professors she encountered when she began her MFA at Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) in 1987. Teachers like Mira Schor and Roni Horn were then challenging the patriarchal bent of contemporary art. While Antoni was shaped by her contact with both artists, the lasting lesson was Schor’s, and it came from outside the classroom. After encouraging Antoni to familiarize herself with the work of other women, Schor sent her student to the library with a list of names. When the catalog failed to yield a scrap or mention of the women cited—as Schor knew it would—her point, about the art world’s marginalization and erasure of women, was made. Schor lent Antoni books from her own library, sparking an informal education in an alternative, feminist history of art. 
	

	From that point on, Antoni began to figure herself in dialogue with earlier generations of women, particularly those active in the ’60s and ’70s, such as Mierle Laderman Ukeles, Carolee Schneemann, Hannah Wilke, and Ana Mendieta. In fact, when she was invited to show at the Wadsworth Atheneum in 1996—the same site where Ukeles had famously presented her Maintenance Art Performance Series in 1973—Antoni chose to repeat Loving Care, implicitly framing her version of floor-cleaning as a work of “maintenance art.”

	Antoni’s first solo exhibition after graduating from RISD was a reckoning with a patriarchal art historical canon, with works undermining masculine-coded formalism through parody and play. Invited by New York gallerist Sandra Gering to produce an installation in her Broome Street space in February 1992, Antoni opted to appropriate Minimalist forms with a feminist twist. Gnaw began with a mold for a straight-edged cube, which she used to cast two blocks, each weighing 600 pounds: One was made from lard and the other from chocolate. The references she was dressing down were clear: The white of the lard suggests Sol LeWitt’s modular cubic frames, while the chocolate surface, mottled by blooms of sugar and fat, approximates the rusted gradations of Tony Smith’s steel Die (1962).
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Antoni removing the mold from a chocolate Lick and Lather bust.
									Photo Christopher Garcia Valle
	



	But Antoni didn’t stop there. With her teeth, she bit brittle mouthfuls from vertices and edges, the serrated enamel tracing grooves in the cubes’ malleable planes. In a 1994 Flash Art interview, she explained, “I was interested in the bite because it’s both intimate and destructive; it sort of sums up my relationship to art history.” She continued, “I feel attached to my artistic heritage and I want to destroy it: It defines me as an artist and it excludes me as a woman, all at the same time.” 

	When it came to discussing Gnaw, Antoni stressed the physicality of her process—especially its stark contrast to the outsourced industrial-scale fabrication common among Minimalist sculptors. The act of biting challenged the cerebral distance of geometric form. Then the expelled chunks of material became the basis for additional objects exhibited in mirrored cases in the rear of the gallery: The lard was combined with beeswax and pigment to produce tubes of lipstick, while the excess chocolate was cast into heart-shaped bonbon boxes. Heightening the work’s oral drive, the Gering Gallery invitation card featured drawn cross-sections of infants suckling at both a woman’s breast and a baby bottle, underscoring Antoni’s embodied approach and emphasis on matrilineal legacies. The following year, the work took its place in the landmark 1993 Whitney Biennial, a show that marked a watershed turn toward social justice and identity politics. 
	

	ANTONI’S EMPHATICALLY PHYSICAL practice soon led her to dance. In the summer of 1996, she was invited by curator France Morin to participate alongside nine other artists in The Quiet in the Land, a monthlong residency at the last active Shaker village, in Sabbathday Lake, Maine. Enmeshed in the community, the artists lived, worked, ate, slept, and attended services alongside their hosts. During the residency, Antoni shot the video Around the World, Around (1996) in the meeting house, inspired by the Shaker practice of ecstatic dance, an extension of their belief that physical labor is a form of prayer. The work opens on a shot of several rows of benches, spindled backrests visible one through the other. The camera shudders gently alongside Antoni’s footsteps, which echo through the space as it meanders over floorboards, a fireplace, and more worn seats. Gradually, she begins to turn, then spin. Windows flash into and out of sight. Her breath comes in fast, static bursts. The camera struggles to focus as her motion picks up speed, until all that we receive are streaks of color and light. Suddenly, we see stillness and a skew angle of woodgrain as she topples and lies straining for breath on the floor.

	Antoni’s work grew even more corporeal following her diagnosis of breast cancer at age 33. By 1999, she had undergone surgery and completed several years of chemotherapy and radiation. Swapping observations on living through cancer with artist Guadalupe Maravilla in a 2021 interview for BOMB magazine, she recalled that ritual was vital to her battle with the disease, that it was “a process that provides the condition for transformation.” She incorporated somatic dance into her daily life; in 2005, she began to regularly attend 5Rhythms, a movement-based meditation practice rooted in gestalt therapy and developed by Gabrielle Roth in the 1970s. She also took classes with Emilie Conrad, who established Continuum Movement, a form of movement therapy that embraces a heightened attunement to the natural world.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Paper Dance, 2013, Antoni’s performance in collaboration with Anna Halprin at the Halprin Dance Deck, Kentfield, Calif.
									Photo Pak Han. Courtesy Luhring Augustine, New York/©Janine Antoni.
	



	“Dance was slowly taking over my entire life,” she told Abigail Levine in a 2016 interview for Movement Research. But, for Antoni, dance was merely another face of visual practice, and it didn’t take long for her to find a way back to sculpture again. In the summer of 2011, Antoni attended a workshop given by Anna Halprin, a pioneering choreographer of postmodern dance, at the Esalen Institute in Big Sur, and soon they were working together. Halprin invited Antoni to perform Paper Dance, Halprin’s improvisational choreography from 1965. The score is simple: Make sounds with paper, crumple and tear it, gather up as much as you can, and leave the stage. What originated as a movement-based and aurally oriented piece became, in Antoni’s hands, durationally drawn and sculptural. Halprin had instructed her, “Just do what you do in the studio with material, and the dance will make itself.” 

	Antoni worked with Halprin over several years before Paper Dance was shown publicly. Over this time, Antoni thought about the intergenerational aspect of the work, noting that it was choreographed when she was an infant. “I was moved by… Anna’s gesture of giving her work away,” she reflected in her studio. “But something else also happened akin to transmission, which I am still trying to understand.” As they worked, Antoni installed a dance floor in her studio, eventually embarking on collaborations with other choreographers, including Stephen Petronio and Annie-B Parson. 
	

	Antoni’s iteration of Paper Dance officially premiered in 2016 at the Fabric Workshop in Philadelphia and was shown again in 2019 at the Contemporary Austin. Attendees sat on and around crates containing Antoni’s past work, visible for some performances and sealed into their wooden armatures for others. In their midst, she moved, drawing with shadow and motion on the impressionable surface of a roll of brown paper, which blended into the nude planes of her skin. She talks of this work as an alternative to a mid-career survey, a history filtered through the lens of flesh. 


			
			
			
	
			
					Saddle, 2000.
	



	BY THE TURN OF THE century, Antoni was equally attuned to the lineage of feminist artists who had charted a path for her as she was to the generation that would follow. From 2000 until 2012, she taught a mentorship course at Columbia University, and spent one week each semester with a group of students in the MFA program. “The whole city was my classroom,” she recalls. “If I teach anything, I teach how to nurture the creative process.” 

	Among her students number multimedia artist Chitra Ganesh, sculptor Aki Sasamoto, and performance and video artist Liz Magic Laser. Laser, who began her career at Columbia in the photography department, remembers an exercise in which members of her cohort each held a cube of ice in their hands until it melted. The activity directly inspired Laser’s first forays into performance, which has remained her primary medium since. 
	

	Antoni’s role as mentor and peer continued with some students beyond their time together at Columbia. Laser attended 5Rhythms sessions with her former professor. Painter Allison Katz worked for several years in her studio, a period Antoni recalls with gratitude: “We wrote and thought together. That’s how I work: I think that my students and assistants have helped me make my work as much as I’ve had any influence on them.”

	Now, Antoni is preparing for her first museum retrospective, opening at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago (MCA) in December of next year. In a recent phone conversation, Joey Orr—MCA Deputy Director and Chief of Curatorial Affairs, co-organizer of the exhibition alongside independent curator Adrian Heathfield—said that while the show will primarily feature sculptures, drawings, photographs, and video, “there’s no way to walk out of the exhibition without having had an experience with the body.” 

	Throughout her career, Antoni has considered how works are physically altered by time and how their resonance shifts in response to different cultural moments. In a 1999 interview with Stuart Horodner for BOMB magazine, she noted that she never saw live versions of some of the works that most influenced her practice: Carolee Schneemann staged Meat Joy (1964) the year Antoni was born, and Joseph Beuys’s I Like America and America Likes Me (1974) took place before she had immigrated to the US. For her, this fact was not entirely negative: She felt that her distance from the works permitted productive misinterpretation. “They become our works through projection,” she observed to Horodner. “I’m interested in how stories get passed down.” And her own works function in a way like performance documentation, objects bearing traces of a past action: For her iconic sculpture Saddle (2000), she cast cowhide over herself while planted on all fours, her body as much an absence as a presence.
	

	The act of working on her own retrospective with the MCA’s curatorial team has pushed Antoni to reconsider her oeuvre. When I asked whether someone else might reperform Loving Care in her place—whether her works are open to the body more generally or are specific to her body in particular—she deliberated. “If you asked me 20 years ago, I would say no. Because all those works were about my relationship to myself.” But then, reflecting on the passage of time and its potential to transform her art, she mused, “I’m looking for new interpretations of the work that honor its past meanings and push them forward to meet our moment.”

	Across writing, painting, and her “trend forecasting” collective K-HOLE, Dena Yago is an armchair theorist of those aesthetic sensibilities so banal and pernicious—so normal and boring—that they could easily go unnoticed. Thrillingly, this makes them all the more fascinating. Yago has turned her attention to such phenomena as the Amazon bags that have become urban tumbleweeds, and to the subtly evolving meanings of ordinary words like “capacity.” Often, when one puts language to a phenomenon, you start to see it everywhere.

	With an artist’s keen eye to the world around her, she has opined on the aesthetics of irony and of cringe, and with her other K-HOLE cofounders, she coined the now ubiquitous term “normcore.” In her paintings, she updates the language of Pop Art to probe the visual culture of late capitalism. A new collection of her writings, That Figures: Selected Writings, is out this month from After 8 Books. For the occasion, Art in America asked her to single out 5 books on her shelf.


			
			
	The Golden Notebook
			
								
				

	By Doris Lessing

	I read The Golden Notebook when I turned 30. A friend gave it to me as a birthday gift, and it took me a while to read, but it’s really special. To me, it’s about how you don’t need to reconcile the political, the economic, the domestic, the maternal, and so on. These things can coexist and weave together. The book made me think about the pressure to reconcile oneself as a political citizen and an artist, versus allowing oneself to be a citizen and also an artist. The protagonist is politically active, and a mother and a writer and all these other things, and all these roles have different expectations.

		
			
			
	Seasonal Associate
			
								
				

	By Heike Geissler

	I’ve always had this book on the reading list when I’ve taught. Geissler worked as a seasonal associate at Amazon, but the book’s conceit is framing it in the second person: You are doing this, you are doing that. It’s one of the best things I’ve read that brings you into the position of being within a logistical infrastructure where you don’t really have agency, and shows what that experience does to your psyche and bodily self.

		
			
			
	The Odd One In: On Comedy
			
								
				

	By Alenka Zupančič

	I read this book right after college, when I went with an artist to the European Graduate School and helped take care of her kid in exchange for taking some of the classes. The author was a student of Slavoj Žižek and is a Nietzsche scholar who has written a lot about comedy.

	The Odd One In is about short-circuiting in comedy, and how different forms of comedy reveal the instability of different structures. With writing, I have a very specific breed of comedy in my own work—an unstable version of it. Comedy reveals the failure of systems and their absurdity, but more specifically their fissures and instabilities. I play with that a lot with language in the visual work I make—for instance the diptych Down for Now and Not for Long. It used phrases from common parlance, but pushed you to read all their valences: a phrase can be optimistic or cynical, containing both.

	Zupančič also writes about slipping on a banana peel, and when I think about the work I did with K-HOLE, a lot of it was about pushing things to their points of failure. You can do that through institutional critique or through comedy.

		
			
			
	Tender Buttons 
			
								
				

	By Gertrude Stein

	I was thinking about the books I have in my studio and reach for often, and Tender Buttons is one. It deals with language as material, letting words expand and contract their meaning. Whenever I get stuck—mostly on poetry or phrasing for visual works—I return to it. In my visual work, I try to pay attention to phrasing or words that take on a cultural significance and bubble up into a different meaning than they had previously. The show I did at JTT in 2023 was called “Capacity” for that reason. It was a word suddenly being used in multiple ways: whether one has the capacity for care, or in the professional sense, as a way of trying to be polite. It evokes a kind of exhaustion. I’m interested in things with multiple meanings

		
			
			
	Pattern Recognition 
			
								
				

	By William Gibson

	The protagonist of Pattern Recognition is a woman named Cayce Pollard, a trend forecaster and brand consultant. I didn’t know that job existed before reading the book in college. It laid out a role I thought I could inhabit. She has a physical reaction to brands: they pay her as a consultant; she walks in, and if the brand is not to her sensibility, she breaks out in hives. Aside from being incredibly cool, she speaks to the embodied aspects of taste. I’m revisiting Gibson’s Spook Country right now for another piece: an essay about logistics, shipping-container aesthetics, and what it all means now.
